*(Speaking as the farmer)*

Alright, let me think this through. I've been doing this since I was in my twenties, so most of it runs by itself now. But with just me and the old lady at home — the kids are gone to the city years ago — I have to watch how much work I take on. That's why I keep the cotton patch small.

This year I'll do it the way I usually do. About 11 mu in wheat-maize double crop on the flatter ground near the village, and around 5 mu of cotton out on the sandier piece. Last year the wheat gave me about 450 kg/mu, maize a bit over 500, cotton around 240 kg lint — so nothing to complain about. No reason to change much.

**Wheat** is already in the ground from last October. I put down about 20 kg urea and a compound fertilizer as base before planting — that's roughly 8 kg N in the base. Irrigated once in winter before the ground froze. Right now in late April the wheat is at jointing, so I'll topdress another 8-9 kg N as urea and water it in. If the grain filling period looks dry in May, I'll give it one more irrigation. The extension guy at the township says 15 kg N is enough but I always put a little more — my ground isn't that rich and I don't want to come up short.

**Maize** goes in right after wheat harvest in mid-June. I don't have time to do much tillage — three, four days between wheat combine and maize planting, that's it. I use the seed-fertilizer drill so the base fertilizer goes in with the seed. Hybrid seed from the township co-op, the Zhengdan variety neighbors have been using. Side-dress urea at the big trumpet stage. If July is dry I irrigate once, otherwise the rains usually take care of it.

**Cotton** is where I spend the most worry. Planting now, late April. It's finicky — needs spraying for bollworm and aphids, and the picking in September-October is brutal with just two of us. I hire two or three people from the village at picking time. I keep the area small for exactly this reason. I grow the Bt hybrid, costs more but saves me several sprays.
